entities.summary:
Henry Marshal was a medieval Dean of York and Bishop of Exeter. Born around 1150, he was the younger son of John Marshal and his wife Sybilla of Salisbury, making him a younger brother of William Marshal and a member of the prominent Marshal family.

As a cleric, Marshal played a crucial role in the governance of the Church in England during the 12th century. He was appointed as the Dean of York in 1176 and later became the Bishop of Exeter in 1188. His tenure as Bishop was marked by significant ecclesiastical reforms, including the promotion of monastic education and the establishment of a new diocesan structure.

Marshal's leadership was also shaped by his involvement in the politics of the time. He was a close advisor to King Henry II and played a key role in the negotiations that led to the Treaty of Lambeth in 1174. This treaty marked a significant turning point in the relations between the English monarchy and the Church, establishing a framework for the Church's relationship with the state that would shape the course of English history for centuries to come.

Despite his significant contributions to the Church and the political landscape of medieval England, Marshal's legacy has been somewhat overshadowed by that of his more famous brother, William Marshal. However, his own achievements as a cleric and statesman remain an important part of the story of medieval England, shedding light on the complex interplay between the Church and the state during a pivotal period in English history.

Henry Marshal died on November 8, 1206, leaving behind a legacy that continues to be felt in the modern era. His work on ecclesiastical reforms and his role as a mediator between the Church and the state have had a lasting impact on the development of the Church in England.
